walkthroughs.body_html:
The Role of Markets and Money — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Role of Markets and Money brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Role of Markets and Money.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A market with one seller is a:
options: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Oligopoly
Monopsony

mcqs.q: The price mechanism performs three functions; which is NOT one?
options: Signalling
Incentivising
Rationing
Producing

mcqs.q: What are the functions of money?
options: Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Money is valuable because it is made of valuable materials.
Medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, and standard of deferred payment — money must perform these to function as money.
Money is only valuable if backed by gold.

mcqs.q: What causes the supply curve to shift?
options: Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
When demand rises, the supply curve shifts right to meet it.
Changes in production costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of producers, expectations — anything affecting supply other than the good's own price.

mcqs.q: What is the principle of comparative advantage?
options: A country should produce whatever it can make best.
Countries should specialise in producing goods with lower opportunity cost relative to others — even a country worse at everything still has a comparative advantage in something.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
Money is only valuable if backed by gold.
